title: Jump Game III
statement: You are given an array `arr` of non-negative integers and stand on index `start`. From index `i` one move takes you to index `i + arr[i]` or to index `i - arr[i]`, but only if that index lies inside the array; you may make any number of moves. Return `true` if some sequence of moves (possibly none) brings you to an index whose value is `0`, and `false` otherwise.
notes:
## Intuition

Treat each index as a node with up to two outgoing edges, to `i + arr[i]` and `i - arr[i]`. The question becomes: does the part of this graph reachable from `start` contain a node whose value is 0? A breadth-first search visits exactly the reachable nodes, each once, so it answers that in linear time. Marking nodes as visited is essential: jumps can lead back and forth forever, and without the marks the search would never stop. (A slower alternative keeps growing a set of reachable indices until a whole pass adds nothing.)

## Approach

1. Mark `start` as visited and put it in `queue`.
2. Take indices from the queue in order, using `head` as the read position.
3. If the current `index` holds 0, a zero is reachable: return `true`.
4. Otherwise look at both jump targets. Each one that is inside the array and not yet visited is marked and added to the queue.
5. When the queue runs out, every reachable index has been checked: return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

`arr = [4,2,3,0,3,1,2]`, `start = 5`.
- Index 5 (value 1): queue 6 and 4.
- Index 6 (value 2): 8 is outside, 4 is already visited.
- Index 4 (value 3): 7 is outside, queue 1.
- Index 1 (value 2): queue 3; -1 is outside.
- Index 3 holds 0, so the answer is `true`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each index enters the queue at most once and has two edges.
- Space: O(n) for `visited` and `queue`.

## Pitfalls

- Mark an index visited when it is queued, not when it is taken out, or it can be queued many times.
- Check both bounds: `next >= 0` and `next < n`.
- `start` itself may already hold 0; the first loop step catches that.
- A jump of length `arr[i]` lands on that exact index; you cannot stop part way.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | length of `arr` |
| `visited` | whether an index has been queued already |
| `queue` | indices waiting to be explored, in BFS order |
| `head` | read position in `queue` |
| `index` | the index being explored |
| `next` | a jump target from `index` |
